transcript.text: washing machine making a horrible noise

Sorry to hear that. A horrible noise from a washing machine can come from a few quite different things, and the type of noise is the biggest clue to which one it is. The most likely causes:
• Unbalanced load: one heavy item like a bath mat, duvet or jeans, or a very small load, makes it bang and shake on spin. This is very common and isn't a fault.
• Installation: if the machine is new or has been moved, the transit bolts in the back might still be in, or it might not be standing level. Either makes it shake and bang badly.
• Something trapped: a coin, hair grip or bra wire caught between the drums gives a metallic tick or scrape. If it's caught in the pump you'd hear a rattle or grind while it empties.
• Worn drum bearings: a deep rumbling or roaring that gets louder as the spin speeds up. This is usually on older machines.
• Suspension or counterweight: heavy banging even with ordinary loads. This is less common. Some quick checks to tell these apart (switch off and unplug first):
1. Think about the load. Was it one heavy item or a small load? If it's fine with a normal mixed load, it was just imbalance.
2. Press down on each top corner. It shouldn't rock. If it does, adjust the foot that isn't touching the floor and tighten its lock nut. If the machine is new or recently moved, check the back panel for large bolts with plastic spacers. If they're there, they need to come out.
3. Open the door and turn the drum slowly by hand. Then push it up and down and rock it. A scraping or tick as it turns points to something trapped. A rough, gritty feel or a drum that clunks and drops suggests bearings. A firm drum with just a little springy movement is normal.
4. Check the pump filter, usually behind a flap at the bottom front. Put towels down and have a shallow tray ready first, as water will come out. Coins and grips often end up in there and rattle. It would really help to know what the noise sounds like and when it happens. Is it banging/shaking, a deep rumble, a metallic tick or scrape, or a grinding rattle? And is it on spin, while it's draining, or all the time? If it's shaking violently or moving across the floor, stop using it until we've worked out why.
[Helpful to see: image "Check the transit bolts have been removed" — Transit bolts hold the drum still for delivery and must be removed before use — a machine that bangs, walks or vibrates (especially when new or recently moved) often still has them fitted. They unscrew from the back of the machine. Typical layout — your machine may differ.]
It's a loud roaring noise on the spin, like a jet engine. Much quieter on the wash. Got worse over a few months. Is it worth fixing?

A roar like a jet engine that gets much louder as the spin speeds up, is quieter on the wash and has slowly worsened over months is a common sign of worn drum bearings. I'm fairly confident, but a quick hand check would confirm it. Is it worth fixing? It depends mainly on age and construction. Bearings are an engineer job: the machine has to be largely stripped to reach the drum. On many modern machines the outer tub is sealed, so the bearings can't be changed on their own and the whole tub assembly has to be replaced. On a mid-range machine more than about 6 to 8 years old, that often costs close to a new machine, so replacing it is usually the better choice. On a newer or higher-end machine, especially one with separately replaceable bearings, repair can be worthwhile. An engineer can tell you which type yours is. Checks to confirm it (switched off and unplugged, door open):
1. Turn the drum slowly by hand. A rough, gritty or rumbling feel points to bearings. A smooth, quiet drum makes them less likely.
2. Grip the top of the drum, lift it and push it down, then rock it. Clunking or noticeable play means worn bearings, or less often a cracked drum spider (the support behind the drum). Firm with only a slight springy give is normal.
3. Look for brown or greasy marks on recent washing, or a dirty, rusty leak under the machine. Either means the bearing seal has failed, which backs up the bearing diagnosis.
4. If the drum feels fine, run an empty spin-only programme. A roar even when empty rules out the load as the cause. If the drum is rough or loose, I'd stop using high spin speeds. Worn bearings get worse, and a dropping drum can rip the door seal or damage the tub, which turns it into a leak. How did the drum feel, and roughly how old is the machine? That will settle whether it's worth repairing.
It's about 9 years old, paid about £350 new. Drum rumbles and grinds when I turn it by hand, and there's clunky up and down play when I lift it. Few brown streaks under the back too.

That settles it. A grinding, rumbling drum by hand, clunky up-and-down play, a roar on spin that has slowly got worse, and brown streaks under the back all point to worn drum bearings. The brown marks are rusty water and grease getting past the failed bearing seal. I'm confident about this. The only other thing that fits is a cracked drum spider (the support behind the drum), which often fails alongside the bearings. Either way the repair is the same scale of job. Is it worth fixing? On a 9-year-old machine that cost about £350, honestly, probably not. 1. Changing the bearings means stripping the machine down to the tub. That's an engineer job, so labour is a big part of the bill.
2. Many machines in that price bracket have a sealed tub. The bearings can't be replaced on their own, so the whole tub and drum assembly has to go in. That often costs close to the price of a new machine.
3. Even with a successful repair, the motor, pump and control board are all nine years old, so you could be paying out again soon. Repair is only really worth it if an engineer finds the tub can be split, so the bearings and seal can be changed separately, and the quote is well under half the cost of a comparable new machine. If you want to know for sure, ask for a quote that says whether the tub is sealed. Otherwise, putting the money towards a replacement is the sensible choice. Until then, you can keep using it for a short while if you need to. Worn bearings eventually let the drum drop, which can tear the seal or damage the tub and cause a proper leak.
